extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, and aesthetes interested in principles of art and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and principles for producing and evaluating art and literary criticism: the aims of art, the nature and methods of criticism, and the temperaments and practices an æsthetic critic or artist should cultivate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of art: create mood / emotion for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: "The aim of art is simply to create a mood." (Art's purpose is emotion for the sake of emotion; art is, in Wilde's phrase, 'immoral'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art should prioritise producing 'beautiful sterile emotions' rather than prompting practical action; examples: the tears at a play are an 'exquisite sterile emotion'. The critic/artist should seek to evoke and shape moods rather than moral or utilitarian outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should purify and initiate without wounding
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art does not hurt us. The tears that we shed at a play are a type of the exquisite sterile emotions that it is the function of Art to awaken... We grieve, but our grief is not bitter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for emotions that 'purify and initiate' the spectator/reader — cathartic but non-destructive. Avoid presenting art as literal suffering or as ethically punitive; prefer emotions that refine sensibility and leave the audience 'not wounded'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art enables vicarious lives — transference of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: We 'sicken with the same maladies as the poets, and the singer lends us his pain' — art lets us live many lives and feel passions and terrors not our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing should facilitate imaginative identification: make readers feel another's joy, grief, shame or passion (examples cited: Fantine, Manon Lescaut, Atys, Orestes, Tyrian). Use concrete narrative and musical language to produce durable vicarious experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination as concentrated race-experience (heredity)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Do you think that it is the imagination that enables us to live these countless lives? Yes: it is the imagination; and the imagination is the result of heredity. It is simply concentrated race-experience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics should recognise imagination as built from collective, inherited cultural memory; draw upon shared traditions and archetypes to broaden imaginative reach and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for the concrete over the vague
rubrics_metrics.description: "To the æsthetic temperament the vague is always repellent... we desire the concrete, and nothing but the concrete can satisfy us."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor tangible, sensory detail and definite images (the visible arts, specific objects, concrete scenes) over abstraction and vague theorising. The concrete grounds moods and makes them persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: The critic is creative and may use many literary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "Who is the true critic but he who bears within himself the dreams... The critic as being in his own way as creative as the artist... The method of the drama is his, as well as the method of the epos."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical writing can and should be imaginative: employ dialogue, narration, fiction, verse, dramatic form, and other modes (examples: Pater's fictional portraits, Ruskin's imaginative prose, Browning's verse-criticism). Use form to reveal rather than merely judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness is not a primary requirement for the critic
rubrics_metrics.description: "A critic cannot be fair in the ordinary sense of the word... it is one's business in such matters to have preferences, and when one has preferences one ceases to be fair."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value passionate, engaged preference over detached impartiality; an 'unbiassed opinion' in art is often valueless. Critics should surrender to the work, allowing strong personal response to guide judgement rather than forced equal admiration of all styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational dispassion is not the critic's ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two ways of disliking art, Ernest. One is to dislike it. The other, to like it rationally... Reason is not the faculty to which it appeals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism grounded solely in rational, dispassionate appraisal misses art's appeal. Allow for 'divine madness' and non-rational response; do not reduce aesthetic judgment to purely logical criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity must be flexible; the critic should change and multiply personalities
rubrics_metrics.description: "A little sincerity is a dangerous thing, and a great deal of it is absolutely fatal... The critic will... be sincere in his devotion to the principle of beauty, but he will seek for beauty in every age and in each school... Through constant change... he will find his true unity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intellectual mobility and willingness to revise positions; avoid being the 'slave of his own opinions'. What looks like 'insincerity' (changing views, multiple moods) is a productive method for critics seeking new sensations and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the spheres of Art and Ethics distinct
rubrics_metrics.description: "The first condition of criticism is that the critic should be able to recognise that the sphere of Art and the sphere of Ethics are absolutely distinct and separate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from moralising art; do not allow ethical prescriptions to be the primary measure of aesthetic value. Beware of journalism and public moralising that confuses ethical judgement with critical assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value contemplation and self-culture over mere practicality
rubrics_metrics.description: "To do nothing at all is the most difficult thing in the world, the most difficult and the most intellectual... It is to do nothing that the elect exist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artists and critics should prioritise contemplative self-culture and intellectual development rather than practical usefulness or busy social reform. Encourage unpractical habits that foster deep thought and refined taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic creation is fundamentally subjective; 'objective' forms are ultimately subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: "All artistic creation is absolutely subjective... the more objective a creation appears to be, the more subjective it really is."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept subjectivity as inevitable and productive in art: even impersonality or 'objective' forms are expressions of the creator's inner life. Use masks, fictional personae, or objective forms as means to reveal inner truths rather than signs of detachment.
